item.title: hoop2vec forecasts: how the numbers get made
item.description:
The day before Kansas hosted Villanova, hoop2vec had Kansas winning 83 to 69, with an 87 percent chance to win. Every game in all four leagues gets a forecast like that: a predicted score, a margin, and a win probability. They’re on each league’s Games page and on every team’s page. A few minutes after a game ends, the ratings and the next forecasts update, and the whole site gets rebuilt from scratch every morning.

The Matchup Lab

The Matchup Lab lets you set up any game yourself. You pick two teams, a site, and the type of game, and the full model runs in your browser. It shows the forecast and what each piece added. For Kansas and Villanova, team strength is worth about 10 points to Kansas, home court and travel add 4, and injuries take away 1. Move the game to a neutral floor and Kansas drops to 81 to 71, with a 77.5 percent chance to win.

The right side compares each team’s offense with the other team’s defense. Villanova’s defense ranks in the 96th percentile against threes and Kansas is about average at shooting them. The site marks that as a defensive edge. Kansas doesn’t take many threes, so it doesn’t move the forecast much.

Ratings

Underneath every forecast are three team ratings. The first is adjusted efficiency, the approach Ken Pomeroy made famous: points scored and allowed per 100 possessions, adjusted for opponent and venue. A possession is one trip down the court. Counting per possession takes pace out of it, so a slow team that wins 60 to 40 doesn’t look worse than a fast team that wins 90 to 70.

The second is a dynamic rating that updates after every game and keeps track of how sure it is. Early in the season it leans on last year’s team and how much of the roster came back. The third is Elo, the system chess uses, which is mostly there as a baseline.

Power, the number each league’s ratings table is sorted by, comes out of the game model. I ask the model how each team would do on a neutral floor against a set of opponents, then shift the scale so an average team lands at zero. In the pros the opponents are every team in the league. In college they’re the top 100. Beating the 350th-best team by 40 doesn’t say much about March.

Players

Player values feed the forecasts too, so the model knows what a team loses when someone sits. Value is how many points per 100 possessions better a team is with a player on the floor than with an average player.

Each league gets it a little differently. Men’s college Value starts from box plus/minus, a standard estimate of a player’s impact from the box score, adjusted for opponents. Early in the season it leans on last season, class, and recruiting ranking. Women’s college basketball doesn’t have the same free player stats, so hoop2vec builds its own box plus/minus from ESPN box scores. The first version gave too much credit to whoever grabbed the rebound or made the shot near the basket, which mostly meant the tallest players. I fixed that by shifting some credit between teammates by height within each game.

The NBA and WNBA use lineups instead. When I tried box plus/minus in the pros, efficient, low-usage centers who rebound and block shots came out as some of the best players in the league. So the pro sites use RAPM, which looks at every stretch where the same ten players were on the floor and works out how much each one moved the score. The box score explains about half of a player’s offensive impact by that measure, and much less of the defense.

Before each game, every player gets a chance of playing, from injury reports and recent missed games. Missed games mean different things in different leagues. A college player who misses a game is usually hurt. Pros rest. An NBA player who’s missed three or more straight games plays the next one only 12 percent of the time. In the first game of the playoffs, that same player plays 76 percent of the time.

The game model

The forecast blends two models. One is a neural network that takes about 40 numbers for each team, from the ratings to shooting, rebounding, turnovers, roster strength, injuries, rest, and travel. It sees both teams at once, so it can pick up on styles that fit together well or badly. The other is a plain linear model built on team ratings, home court, travel, rest, and injuries. It can’t learn matchups, but it’s harder to fool.

The backtest picks how much weight each one gets. In men’s college basketball and the NBA, the network gets 70 percent. In the women’s college game it gets 80. The WNBA has 15 teams and short seasons, so there isn’t much data, and the backtest gives the linear model 70 percent there instead.

To test it, I had each league’s model predict every past game as if it were the morning of the game. It could only learn from earlier seasons, and it only saw injury news that was public before tip-off. For men’s college basketball that’s about 82,000 games since 2012, and the model picked the winner in 73.5 percent of them. The score I care more about is log loss, which punishes a confident wrong forecast much harder than an unsure one. In men’s and women’s college basketball and the NBA, the blend beat each of its parts and every rating it’s built from. The WNBA’s history is short enough that the models all land within noise of each other.

The toughest comparison is a sportsbook. ESPN carries closing betting lines for some games, and they’re more accurate than hoop2vec in men’s college basketball and the NBA. The gap is bigger in the NBA, where the betting market is sharper. In women’s college basketball hoop2vec slightly beats the few lines ESPN carries. Those markets are thinner, so that’s believable, but I don’t make much of it.

Around 2020 I spent a lot of my free time trying to beat the stock market, predict elections, and model sports betting. What I found is that an actual edge comes from data other people don’t have. A model built on public data usually ends up close to the betting line and a little behind it. hoop2vec is no exception.

Brackets, playoffs, and the draft

The college sites project the 76-team NCAA tournaments until Selection Sunday, then switch to the real brackets. hoop2vec works out each team’s odds of reaching each round exactly, without simulating, because it has a win probability for every possible game. Even the best men’s team usually has well under a 50 percent chance to win it all, since it has to win six straight games against good teams. There also aren’t enough tournament games to tell models apart. In 936 past men’s tournament games, every reasonable model I tested landed within noise of the others.

The pro sites play out the rest of the regular season 10,000 times, then apply the tiebreakers, the NBA play-in, and each league’s playoff format. In past NBA playoff series, hoop2vec did a fair amount better than just picking the team with home court.

The college sites also have a Prospects page with two models. One estimates each player’s chance of being drafted in each tier, from the top 5 down to getting picked at all. The other estimates the chance a player becomes a real contributor in the pros. In testing, an average of 20 of the model’s top 30 players were drafted, compared with about 15 for a simple baseline. Pro teams are still better at this than I am. They get workouts, medical reports, and interviews, and I get box scores.

Each league has a Method page with the details and every backtest number, including the ones where the sportsbook wins.

item.title: hoop2vec teams: clicking on Kansas
item.description:
Every team name on hoop2vec is a link. Click one and you get a page with just about everything the site knows about that team. Click a player on that page and you get their career. I’ll use Kansas for this, partly because they’re good this year and partly because I went to grad school there. The screenshots are from the morning of November 26, seven games into the season.

The top of the page

The header has the basics. Kansas is No. 11 in Power, plays in the Big 12, and is 6-1. The red badge says injuries are costing them about a point per 100 possessions right now. The other three badges are the team’s identity, which I’ll get to.

Power is the main rating. It’s how many points per 100 possessions a team would beat an average Division I team by on a neutral floor. A possession is one trip down the court, and Kansas averages about 72 of them a game. So +30.4 works out to beating an average team by about 22 points.

The next three tiles split that up. Kansas scores 121.0 points per 100 possessions and allows 95.1, both adjusted for who they played and where. Tempo is possessions per 40 minutes. The dynamic rating is a second rating that updates after every game and keeps track of how sure it is. The ±5.3 is that uncertainty, and in November it’s pretty wide. Roster strength adds up the player values on the roster, weighted by minutes.

The last two tiles turn Power into odds. Kansas would beat an average team on a neutral floor 90 percent of the time. Against a typical top-25 team it’s a coin flip.

How they play

The identity card describes how a team plays, separately from how good it is. Kansas comes out as Mid-Range Shot-Makers on offense, Contain, Don’t Foul on defense, and Small-Ball Guards for personnel. Each label has a match percentage and a runner-up. Kansas is a 49 percent match for Mid-Range Shot-Makers and 31 percent for Downhill Rim Attack.

The labels come from play-by-play data, which logs every shot, rebound, turnover, foul, and substitution. hoop2vec computes a few dozen rates for every team, takes out the part that’s just team quality, and groups the rest into style dimensions. The badge at the top says “Low confidence” because seven games isn’t much, so early cards still lean on last season.

Right below the card is a list of strengths. The first one says Kansas lives at the rim, with 43.9 percent of its shots there. That sits right under an offense labeled Mid-Range Shot-Makers. Both are true. Kansas takes fewer threes than 93 percent of teams. Almost everything else is a two, either at the rim or from mid-range. The vulnerabilities box says “No clear weak spots yet.” I’d give that a few more weeks.

The matchup notes list Contain, Don’t Foul defenses as both a matchup Kansas should like and one to watch out for. Those defenses give up transition chances, which Kansas likes. They also take away free throws, which Kansas also likes.

Further down, each dimension gets a slider. The blue dot is the season, the orange dot is the last eight games or so, and the shaded band is the uncertainty. Kansas plays a deep rotation, at the 92nd percentile, and gives very few minutes to traditional big men. Below the sliders is a table with the raw numbers behind them. Kansas gives 9 percent of its minutes to traditional bigs, compared with 21 percent for the average team.

Style barely helps predict games once you know how good both teams are. So the cards are there to describe teams, and the forecasts mostly leave them alone.

Roster and schedule

The roster table lists every player with their minutes and their Value. Value is how many points per 100 possessions better a team is with that player on the floor than with an average player. It’s split into offense and defense. Trey Kaufman-Renn leads Kansas at +8.0.

The last column is availability, the chance a player plays in the next game. It comes from injury reports and recent missed games. Tyran Stokes is listed as probable with an ankle injury, which the site turns into 90 percent. Further down the table, out of frame, Melvin Council Jr. is at 0 percent. He’s most of the reason for the injury badge in the header.

The schedule shows every game. Finished games have the score and the win probability the model gave before tip-off. Kansas beat Kentucky as a 68 percent favorite and lost to Houston at 37 percent. Upcoming games have the current win probability and predicted margin.

Clicking on a player

Every name in the roster is a link. Kaufman-Renn’s page starts with the same kind of tiles as the team page. His Value of +8.0 ranks 23rd in Division I. Impact is Value adjusted for playing time. It’s what he adds to the team’s rating compared with a replacement-level player, the kind any team could find at the end of its bench. His is +6.2, 51st in the country.

Then comes the shot chart. Each dot is a spot on the floor, and bigger dots mean more attempts. The color compares his shooting in that zone with the Division I average. The table next to it has the numbers. He’s made 18 of 23 at the rim and 12 of 22 from short mid-range, both way above average. That short mid-range shot is 39 percent of his attempts, compared with 13 percent for a typical player. So the team’s Mid-Range Shot-Makers label has a face.

You can switch the chart from exact locations to zones, or pick an earlier season. Exact spots only go back a couple of college seasons, because that’s when ESPN started logging where college shots came from. Before that it’s zones.

At the bottom is the career table, with a row for every season. Kaufman-Renn spent four years at Purdue before transferring. As a junior he scored 20.1 points a game and used 31.1 percent of Purdue’s possessions while he was on the floor. At Kansas he’s scoring less, using less, and posting the best box plus/minus of his career. Box plus/minus is a standard estimate of a player’s impact from the box score. His is +10.3, but his Value is +8.0, because hoop2vec pulls a seven-game sample back toward what it expected coming into the year.

Men’s college careers go back to 2007-08 and come from Bart Torvik’s player tables. Women’s college careers go back to 2018-19, and NBA and WNBA careers go back to 2008, playoffs included. Those come from ESPN box scores. Every player in all four leagues has a page like this, which is a little over 10,000 shot charts.

item.title: Introducing hoop2vec
item.description:
hoop2vec is a basketball ratings and forecasting site. It covers four leagues: men’s and women’s Division I, the NBA, and the WNBA. Every team gets a new rating a few minutes after each of its games ends, and the whole thing is rebuilt from scratch every morning. Every game gets a forecast, and every player gets a value. All of it comes from free public data.

Each league has the same set of pages. There’s a ratings table, a list of games with forecasts, a players table, and a Matchup Lab where you can pit any two teams against each other at any site. Every team has its own page, and so does every player, with career stats and a shot chart. The college sites add NBA or WNBA draft projections and a projected NCAA tournament bracket. The pro sites have playoff odds instead. The next post walks through a team page, and the one after that covers how the forecasts get made.

How it compares

There are a bunch of good basketball sites already. Most cover one league, and some of the best parts cost money. This is how hoop2vec lines up with the ones I use most, as of November 2026. Men’s and Women’s are Division I. Odds means bracket or playoff odds, and Code means the code is public. A check means free, a dollar sign means paid, and an X means the site doesn’t offer it.

Site Men’s Women’s NBA WNBA Ratings Forecasts Players Odds Code
hoop2vec ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓
KenPom $ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ $ $ ✗ ✗
Bart Torvik ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗
EvanMiya ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ $ ✓ ✓ ✗
Haslametrics ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓ ✗ ✓ ✗
ESPN BPI ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓ ✗ ✓ ✗
Her Hoop Stats ✗ ✓ ✗ ✓ $ $ ✓ ✓ ✗
Dunks & Threes ✗ ✗ $ ✗ $ $ $ $ ✗

A check doesn’t mean equal quality. KenPom and Torvik have years of trust that hoop2vec hasn’t earned, and nobody has tested hoop2vec head to head against them. EvanMiya’s college player ratings are more sophisticated than mine, and so are Dunks & Threes’ NBA ones. A sharp sportsbook still beats hoop2vec during the regular season.

What hoop2vec has is coverage. It’s the only site on the list with all four leagues, and the only one where you can read the code behind every number.

The name is a nod to word2vec, a method that learns a short list of numbers for each word based on the words around it. hoop2vec’s game model does something loosely similar for teams. It learns a list of numbers for each one and uses them to score how any two teams fit together. That’s close enough for me to keep the name.

Why basketball

I used to be a big San Antonio Spurs fan, starting with David Robinson and going through the Tim Duncan years. As I write this, hoop2vec has the Spurs at No. 1 in the NBA. I didn’t touch anything.

Then I went to graduate school at the University of Kansas, where I tutored players on the men’s and women’s basketball teams and went to a bunch of games. I live in Michigan now, and I still crave Free State Brewing Company and Burger Stand about once a week. My favorite college team is the correct favorite team. These days I like pretty much all basketball.

Most of my modeling has been on men’s college basketball, on and off for about ten years, going back to a college basketball dataset I put on data.world. I’ve tried to predict upsets. I’ve tried strange hybrids of Bayesian models, latent variable models, Elo, XGBoost, and a transformer fine-tuned on press coverage. A few of them filled out my brackets. I usually compared them against KenPom, and mostly what I learned is how simple and effective KenPom is. The site still looks like it’s from the 90s, though.

I’ve always wanted a free site that shows advanced stats and is easy to get around, for every league and not just men’s college basketball. That’s what hoop2vec is trying to be.

How it got built

From about 2014 to 2020 I was making things all the time and sharing most of them, a lot of it on Twitter. Some of it was academic and some of it was just for fun. Then COVID hit, I had my first kid, and I changed careers. Now there are two young kids at home, and side projects pretty much stopped.

What’s different now is that I can do this kind of work from my phone. I describe what I want to Claude Code, it writes the code, and I read what it did and push back. Most of hoop2vec got built that way, a few minutes at a time.

It started as two separate men’s college projects. On the first, I described what I wanted and how I thought it should be done, then let Claude Code build it and propose improvements. The second I directed much more strictly. Then I merged the good ideas from both, keeping whichever piece tested better where they overlapped. Once that worked, I carried the same approach over to the women’s game, the NBA, and the WNBA.

I’m not totally comfortable working this way. I like control, and I like knowing how every piece works. I have less of that here than I’d want. But I’ve spent years building up expertise in analytics and data science, and this lets me use it a lot faster than typing everything myself.
